deep.reconstruction:
CONTEXT (previous page). y is a single-valued algebraic function of x with f(y,x)=0, where f has integer coefficients. y is assumed rational for every rational x in α ≤ x ≤ β, with α=p/q and β=r/s rational. The Möbius substitution x=(pt+r)/(qt+s) maps t∈[0,∞) onto the interval and turns f into g(y,t). Hilbert first treats the binomial case g = ψ y^n − φ(t). Putting z = ψ y gives z^n = χ(t), a polynomial with deg χ = n·m.

LINES 1-2. The symbol transcribed '4' is almost certainly Hilbert's 't'.
- Dividing z^n = χ(t) by t^{mn} gives (z/t^m)^n = χ(t)/t^{mn} = a_0 + a_1(1/t) + ... + a_{mn}(1/t^{mn}). The crossed-out start is presumably a_0·1/t^0.
- Taking n-th roots (my filling): z/t^m = a_0^{1/n}(1 + (a_1/a_0)(1/t) + ...)^{1/n} = α_0 a_0^{1/n} + α_1(1/t) + ... . This is a convergent expansion of each branch at t=∞ in integral powers of 1/t. Hilbert's α_0 is a root of unity selecting the branch.
- 'Likewise the other n roots, where one may have to choose other (rational) leading terms etc.' This is the standard step in Hilbert's irreducibility method: expand the branches at infinity and show that a branch taking rational values at the relevant points must have rational coefficients and finitely many terms, i.e. be rational.

SATZ I. If an algebraic function of x is rational at all rational x between α and β, it is necessarily a rational function of x with rational coefficients.

SATZ II. Same conclusion if it is rational at all positive integers x. Hilbert abbreviates the shared hypothesis with dashes.

GENERAL CASE. If z does not satisfy a binomial equation, take an arbitrary one, z^n + a_1 z^{n-1} + ... + a_n = 0 (a first attempt with y is crossed out).
- The a_i are written as forms in (p,q), homogenising t=p/q.
- Setting q=0 gives z=α; 'for all p it follows z − p^ν', i.e. growth like p^ν, 'hence n = νμ etc.'
- This is a fragmentary sketch, presumably comparing orders of growth at infinity (branch exponents). It is not a complete argument.

SECOND TOPIC: the concept of continuity of a function of one real variable. Hilbert lists possible patterns:
- 0) everywhere continuous;
- 1) continuous except at one point;
- 2) discontinuous everywhere except one point (my example, not on the page: x·D(x), D the Dirichlet function, continuous only at 0);
- 3) discontinuous on an everywhere-dense set, continuous elsewhere. His example is f(p/q)=1/q for p,q coprime and f(x)=0 for irrational x. This is Thomae's function, discontinuous exactly at the rationals and continuous at the irrationals.

The next page continues this: discontinuity sets supposedly countable, so no function is continuous exactly on the rationals.
errors: Satz I/II need the algebraic function to be defined over Q (integer coefficients in f, as fixed on the previous page) and to be a single-valued branch. With these the statements are correct and follow from Hilbert's irreducibility theorem. The page itself gives only the expansion step, not a proof.

The leading coefficient should be ζ·a_0^{1/n} (ζ an n-th root of unity) to cover all n branches. Hilbert's α_0 presumably plays this role. Rationality of a_0^{1/n} etc. is asserted ('etc.'), not proved here.
The general (non-binomial) case is only a fragmentary sketch ('z − p^ν', 'n = νμ etc.'); no rigorous argument is given.
In Thomae's function, rationals must be written with q>0 in lowest terms (f(0)=1). The page omits this, which is harmless.

Context, next page: the claim that the set of discontinuity points 'must necessarily be countable' is false in general. Discontinuity sets are exactly the F_sigma sets and can be uncountable, e.g. the indicator of the Cantor set. The conclusion that no function is continuous exactly at the rationals is nevertheless true (Volterra 1881 / Baire category). The proposed proof via ordering by oscillation Δ only shows each set {osc ≥ 1/k} is closed.

results.what: An algebraic function (over Q) taking rational values at all rational points of an interval, or at all positive integers, is a rational function with rational coefficients. The method uses expansion of branches at t=∞ in powers of 1/t after a Möbius change of variable.
results.modern_name: Hilbert's irreducibility theorem (corollary form); proof via Puiseux/Laurent expansion at infinity
results.usually_credited_to: David Hilbert, 'Über die Irreducibilität ganzer rationaler Functionen mit ganzzahligen Coefficienten', J. reine angew. Math. 110 (1892)

results.what: Expansion (z/t^m) = (χ(t)/t^{mn})^{1/n} = ζ a_0^{1/n} + α_1/t + ... of the branches of z^n=χ(t) at infinity
results.modern_name: Laurent/Puiseux expansion of an algebraic function at infinity (binomial case)

results.what: Classification of continuity patterns, including a function discontinuous at every rational and continuous at every irrational: f(p/q)=1/q, f(irrational)=0

deep.surprise_reason: The algebraic part is a working draft of Hilbert's own irreducibility theorem (published 1892, credited to him). It is of genetic/historical interest (Satz I/II, binomial case via expansion at infinity) but not new attribution. The continuity part reproduces Thomae's known example.

checkable.sympy: t,a0,a1,a2=symbols('t a0 a1 a2',positive=True); series((a0+a1/t+a2/t**2)**Rational(1,3), t, oo, 3)
checkable.asserts: The branch (χ(t)/t^{mn})^{1/n} expands at t=∞ as a0^(1/n) + c1/t + c2/t^2 + ... in integral powers of 1/t (illustrated for n=3).
For deg χ = n*m (here n=2, m=2), χ(t)/t^{nm} = a0 + a1/t + ... + a_{nm}/t^{nm}, giving the identity (z/t^m)^n = Σ a_k t^{-k}.

checkable.sympy: p,q,r,s,t=symbols('p q r s t',positive=True); x=(p*t+r)/(q*t+s); (limit(x,t,0), limit(x,t,oo))
checkable.asserts: The substitution x=(pt+r)/(qt+s) maps t=0 to r/s and t=∞ to p/q, so t∈[0,∞) parametrizes the interval between β=r/s and α=p/q.
sqrt(x) is rational at all perfect squares but is not a rational function, so the full hypotheses of Satz I/II (all rationals in an interval / all integers) are needed.

checkable.sympy: from sympy import Rational; f=lambda r: Rational(1,Rational(r).q); [f(Rational(k,12)) for k in range(1,12)]
checkable.asserts: Thomae's function values f(p/q)=1/q in lowest terms; at irrationals f=0, giving continuity at irrationals and discontinuity at rationals.
